\section*{Monte Carlo: the limit law at the named design}

\emph{Section numbers throughout this document refer to the article}; this
document's own headings carry no numbers. This section is the first of the
article's four Monte Carlo experiments, the one run at the configuration the
theory names. It adds no result: the text is the article's, moved here
unchanged except for the cross-references a move breaks, and the floats are the
ones it used to print. The section that follows carries the design validation
underneath it.
The design is the one the theory names, and naming it is also the concession. At
$(\mu,s,a,\alpha)=(2,3,\tfrac34,0.32)$ the frontier holds, $\kappa\alpha=0.256$
exceeding $\tfrac14$, and the turn computed in Section 4 of the article falls at
$n^{\ast}\approx10^{58}$. The experiment therefore runs where the theorem is true
and where its asymptotics are known in advance not to bind. Both laws draw a
two-valued instrument, $\mathsf L=2$. \Cref{thm:rootn} is stated at general finite
$\mathsf L$ and is asymptotic in $n$ at fixed $\mathsf L$, with no claim of
uniformity in the cardinality, so nothing in the limit law itself turns on it;
how large the remainder is at a given $n$ is a different question, and the two
sections that follow measure it rather than assume it away.

One hypothesis of \cref{thm:rootn} is imposed by none of the designs below, and
whether it holds anyway is a question about the design rather than about the
anchor. Every design builds its debiasing weight on the zero anchor, which
\cref{rem:anchor} admits with no further assumption, and setting the anchor to zero leaves $E[L_\star\mid\Delta Z]$ at
whatever the design makes it. On the two laws run here it makes it zero at
$\mathsf L=2$ and not at $\mathsf L=4$, which are the two cardinalities that
check is run at on those laws. All of the solved representer's
coefficient energy sits on odd $q$ at the binary cardinality, where the
antiderivative basis is odd in $u$, so $L_\star$ is odd in $u$, and $\Delta U$ is
independent of $(\Delta Z,W)$ by construction and symmetric about zero, so the
conditional mean vanishes by parity. Computed in population rather than
estimated, the largest entrywise defect is $3.3\times10^{-6}$ of $\|L_\star\|$ at
$\mathsf L=2$ against $0.191$ at $\mathsf L=4$ (\cref{tab:sim-n1defect}). The
binary arms therefore run inside the hypothesis in the propensity direction,
which is the direction \cref{prp:orthog}(iii) prices, and the four-cell panel of
the cardinality arm does not. \emph{That settles the N1 clause of \textup{(T-2)} and
not \textup{(T-2)} entire}, whose A2 and A$2'$ clauses nothing here certifies,
and it settles it on the two laws of this section and of the
cardinality arm; Design H of the next section runs the same anchor at $\mathsf L=2$ and was not
put through the population check. What the failure costs is measured in the
cardinality arm. The multinomial designs of the last of these Monte Carlo sections carry that
check at three cardinalities and fail it at all of them
(\cref{tab:sim-multinomial-n1defect}). \emph{That measurement is taken at the weight
the engine solves for and not at $\ell_\star$}, which is the qualification that
section states where it makes it, and it does not show that
$\ell_\star$ fails N1 on those designs.

What we can measure is the size of the gap and the speed at which it closes.

We run two data-generating laws, DGP A and DGP B, the second harsher in its
geometry, at a condition number of $27.7$ against $3.6$ (\cref{tab:supp-dgpvalid}), and its linearisation residual larger at every $n$
(\cref{tab:sim-limitlaw}, and drawn in \cref{fig:sim-linresid}). The limit-law arm
goes to $n=181{,}019$ at $5{,}000$ replications in every cell; the
$\varphi$-step arm runs $36$ cells at $n\in\{500,2{,}000,8{,}000\}$ and $300$
replications, sweeping $\mathsf c_{14}$ over four decades. Monte Carlo error is
fixed before any gap is read: the coverage standard error is $0.0031$ at the
$95\%$ level and $0.0042$ at the $90\%$, the standard-deviation-ratio standard
error lies between $0.0099$ and $0.0208$, and precision does not vary with $n$.
Everything below is produced by \texttt{scripts/simulations/sim\_thm\_rootn\_run\_all.R}.

The verdict is that the estimator matches its limit law at large $n$ only.

Write $c_\delta$ for the constant in A5(ii)'s $O_P(\delta_n)$. At $c_\delta=0.25$
the ratio of the simulated standard deviation to its asymptotic value fails a
two-standard-error bar at every $n\le64{,}000$ in DGP A, at $16.90$, $8.30$,
$5.83$, $4.93$, $3.09$, $3.37$ and $2.82$ standard errors, and clears it only at
$n=181{,}019$ (\cref{tab:sim-seunits}). In DGP B the worst studentised
quantile is still $2.92$ standard errors off there
(\cref{fig:sim-qq}, and \cref{tab:supp-quantiles}).

or $9.18$ standard errors below nominal. Coverage at that level is below nominal
in $8$ of $8$ cells of DGP A, at a sign-test $p$ of $0.0078$, with every cell
beyond three standard errors (\cref{tab:sim-limitlaw}).

Both configurations satisfy identical hypotheses, and we have no ground on which
to set the failing one aside.

What separates them is the constant, quadratically. Dividing the $c_\delta=1$
distortion by $16$ reproduces the observed $c_\delta=0.25$ ratio to within two
standard errors at every $n\ge22{,}627$. The distortion at the smaller constant is
not absent. It is the same remainder, divided by sixteen.

Three statistics isolate the theorem itself, and none is in doubt. The
linearisation residual, taken per replication so that nothing cancels across
replications, decreases monotonically in all four core panels, from $1.015$ to
$0.319$ in DGP A at $c_\delta=0.25$ (\cref{fig:sim-linresid}). The distance
between the sample sandwich and its limit does the same, from $1.227$ to $0.096$.
An ablation at exact nuisances gives $0.147$, $0.052$ and $0.019$ at
$n=1{,}000$, $8{,}000$ and $64{,}000$, ratios of $2.83$ and $2.74$ against
$\sqrt8=2.828$, with coverage $0.951$, $0.948$ and $0.952$
(\cref{tab:sim-ablation}).

So the gaps are the remainder and not the theorem. They track
$\sqrt n\,\delta_n^{2}$, which on this grid rises in $n$ and does not fall below
one until $n\approx10^{394}$ (\cref{tab:sim-crossings}; the ledger it is computed
from is \cref{tab:supp-budget}). What describes any
feasible sample is the rate-floor corollary of Section 4 of the article.

prices that dependence. Source:

\texttt{paper/tables/sim/sim\_thm\_rootn\_crossings.tex}.
\end{tablenotes}
\end{threeparttable}
\end{table}

The mean-zero injection of the structural error was an idealisation, and it is
now measured (\cref{tab:supp-bias}). At $c_\delta=1$ and the largest $n$,
interpolating to a fully deterministic error at the same $L^{2}(\pi)$ norm
improves the standard-deviation ratio from $18.85$ to $6.78$ standard errors and
worsens $95\%$ coverage from $-8.08$ to $-9.65$. The centring moves across the
whole table and not only there: under a mean-zero draw it stays within $1.92$
standard errors of zero in all eight cells, and under a deterministic one it
reaches $2.04$ to $5.51$ in the four $c_\delta=1$ cells while staying within
$1.6$ in the four at $c_\delta=0.25$. The idealisation was concealing a location
distortion and not a scale one, and it was concealing it mostly at the larger
constant.

The $\varphi$-step arm measures the stopping rule of Section 3 of the article, and its finding
concerns the criterion rather than the constant. Write
$\hat r(m):=\hat{\mathcal A}_{\hat\varphi^{(0)}}v_m
+\hat T_{h_x}(\hat\varphi^{(0)},\theta)$ for the residual of the stage-one linear
equation at Landweber pass $m$, measured in $L^{2}(\Pi)$, which is the quantity
\cref{def:lfstep}(c) compares to its level; $\hat r(0)$ is that residual at the
start $v_0=0$. Over the whole admissible budget the discrepancy criterion falls
by $11$ to $43$ per cent, the ratio
$\|\hat r(\bar m_n)\|/\|\hat r(0)\|$ running from $0.57$ to $0.89$
(\cref{tab:sim-stopping}, Panel B). A threshold therefore sits above the criterion at
one step, or below it at the cap, unless it lands in a window between $0.06$ and
$0.27$ decades wide, which is $1$ to $7$ per cent of the four decades swept.

The stop is then decided by $\mathsf c_{14}$ and not by the data. The cap is
returned in every replication of all twelve cells at $\mathsf c_{14}\le10^{-3}$,
one step is taken in every replication of all twelve at
$\mathsf c_{14}\ge10^{-1}$, and in exactly one of the $36$ cells the interior
branch is the largest of the three shares, at $n=8{,}000$ under the zero
preliminary and $\mathsf c_{14}=10^{-2}$, where it takes $0.543$ of the
replications against $0.347$ at the cap and $0.110$ at one step. The interior
branch carries an outright majority there and nowhere else, and the majority is
a point estimate rather than a separation: its Monte Carlo standard error is
$0.029$, so $0.543$ clears a half by $1.5$ of them. That window moves with $n$,
from $(0.022,0.026)$
at $n=500$ to $(0.0089,0.016)$ at $n=8{,}000$ under the zero preliminary, so no
fixed $\mathsf c_{14}$ is stable in $n$ (\cref{tab:sim-stopping}, Panel B;
\cref{fig:supp-stopping} draws the sweep).

What the printed panels support is narrower than the sweep they summarise. The
$36$ cells are the whole of it and Panel B prints six, at
$\mathsf c_{14}=10^{-2}$; the frequencies are non-degenerate at two of the six
swept values, $10^{-2}$ and $3\times10^{-2}$, and only the first is printed, the
remaining four being the degenerate columns just described. Panel A reports the
\emph{median} stopped iteration, so a cell reading $1$ or reading the cap does
not by itself establish what every replication did; the branch frequencies that
do are Panel B's.

Why the criterion barely moves is visible beside it:
$\omega_n/\|\hat{\mathcal A}\|$ lies between $329{,}694$ and $679{,}332$, so one
Landweber pass is numerically invisible and the cap exceeds $\hat\delta_n^{-2}$
by a factor of $7.32\times10^{8}$ to $2.78\times10^{9}$
(\cref{tab:sim-stopping}, Panel C).

A Lepskii-balanced stop was run alongside, and the comparison splits by
preliminary. Given the discrepancy rule its own oracle $\mathsf c_{14}$, an
advantage no analyst can take because that constant is not identified, Lepskii
is ahead in all three cells started from zero and behind in all three started
from a rate-accurate preliminary. The margins are not all read the same way. In
the two zero-preliminary cells at $n=500$ and $n=2{,}000$ the discrepancy arm
returns $\|\vdagger\|=0.7071$ in every replication, so the paired standard error
of the difference is exactly the Lepskii arm's: at $n=500$ the gap is $0.0048$
against a standard error of $0.0062$, which is $0.77$ standard errors and is not
a win, and at $n=2{,}000$ it is $0.0335$ against $0.0032$, which is $10.6$ on the
unrounded gap and standard error and $10.5$ on the four digits printed. In
the remaining four cells both arms vary and their covariance is not stored, so
we report the bound that holds whatever it is,
$\mathrm{SE}\le\mathrm{SE}_{\mathrm{Lep}}+\mathrm{SE}_{\mathrm{DP}}$: the
zero-preliminary gap at $n=8{,}000$ is at least $6.9$ standard errors, and the
three rate-accurate cells go the other way by at least $6.6$, $3.6$ and $3.8$.
At a fixed $\mathsf c_{14}=3\times10^{-2}$, read at that cell in both arms,
Lepskii is ahead in all six by at least $1.9$ to $6.9$ on the same bound
(\cref{tab:sim-stopping}, Panel D, columns 7 and 8, the two headed at
$3\times10^{-2}$).

The win is unflattering where it happens. The oracle constant in every
rate-preliminary cell is $10^{-1}$ or $1$, values at which one step is taken in
every replication, so the rule wins by returning the injected preliminary out of
a budget of $10^{10}$ to $10^{11}$ steps. In every zero-preliminary cell the same
prescription returns an error of exactly $\|\vdagger\|=0.7071$ and loses. The
oracle does not separate the two preliminaries: the prescriptions coincide at
$10^{-1}$ at $n=2{,}000$, sit at $10^{-1}$ against $1$ at $n=500$, which are both
values at which one step is taken, and differ in kind only at $n=8{,}000$, where
the zero preliminary prefers $3\times10^{-2}$. One constant is therefore best
under both preliminaries at the two smaller sample sizes while returning an
estimate under one of them and nothing under the other, and nothing in the data
chooses it in any case.

Four things this exercise does not do should be read with it. No constructed
$\hat\ell$ is tested, because none exists to test. The realised operator is more
ill-posed than H1 admits, its fitted decay index running from $1.63$ to $2.14$
against the $0.75$ of the design, and the injected error occupies six Fourier
modes that the operator damps by a factor between $2.64$ and $5.36$, so no error
in the damped directions is exhibited. \cref{tab:supp-condition} prints the
index and the damping; the mode count is a constant of the injection basis, and
the notes to that table read the damping off against the spectrum, at most a
tenth of it in log terms. And no law violating an assumption is
run, so a match is a non-rejection by a procedure shown able to reject only
through the $-\hat J^{-1}$ counterfactual and the $c_\delta$ contrast (\cref{tab:supp-jacobian}).

Two quantities are unavailable rather than reported. Both condition numbers sit
at the double-precision floor and are printed as lower bounds, and at $n=2{,}000$
the quadrature caps the Gram's rank at $780$ of $2{,}000$ (\cref{tab:supp-condition}, Panel A).

The index measure is implemented as a quadrature and not as counting measure, and
the distinction is not bookkeeping: counting measure overstates the cap inflation
by a factor of $2.93$, which is the node count divided by the volume of
$\mathcal T$ and so is arithmetic on two constants of the configuration rather
than a measurement. At the twelve-node grid the normalising constant is still
$16$ per cent below and the cap $29$ per cent below their exact values, a
convergent quadrature error we declare rather than absorb; that pair is read off
a refinement run and appears in no table.

An applied reader should take three things from this section, all of them
statements at $\mathsf L=2$. The estimator runs,
is correctly signed, and its remainder accounting is complete for nuisance errors
of the priced size. Its normal approximation is accurate at $n=181{,}019$ at one
of two equally admissible constants, and at neither constant below $n=64{,}000$.
Nominal $90\%$ intervals under-cover at $29$ of the $32$ cells, the three
exceptions clearing nominal by less than one Monte Carlo standard error, and a
panel of the size
this readership has is described by the rate floor and not by the $\sqrt n$
statement. The cardinality scoping is not decoration: the section on cardinality below
finds the first of the three failing at $\mathsf L=4$ on this same design.

\section*{Monte Carlo: supplementary tables and figures}

This section carries the design validation and the cell-level detail behind the
experiment above. It adds no result. What follows is the validation of the two
laws, the cell-level detail underneath two of the preceding section's summary
tables, the ledger its extrapolations are computed from, the diagnostics of the
$\varphi$-step arm, and the verification of the Jacobian. \emph{The opening
sentence of this paragraph named the article and not the section above until
2026-08-27}, when the experiment it validates moved here; a framing sentence
that survives the thing it frames is the defect this project keeps finding, so
it was rewritten rather than left. Every table is
produced by \texttt{scripts/simulations/sim\_thm\_rootn\_run\_all.R} and the file
it is read from is named in its notes.

\section*{Monte Carlo: the design with frontier headroom}

This section carries the second Monte Carlo experiment of the article, the one
run at Design H, together with its supplementary material. It adds no result.
The experiment opens the section, in the article's own text and with its own two
floats: the remainder budget both designs realise, with the contrast between
them, and the outcome against the pre-committed criterion. What follows them is
the configuration behind those two floats, the validation of the two laws drawn
from it, the ledger the budget is read off, and the cell-level detail underneath
the summary. \emph{Through 2026-08-27 this paragraph said the article printed
the two floats}, which it did until that pass moved them here. Every table is
produced by
\texttt{scripts/simulations/sim\_thm\_rootn\_headroom.R} and the file it is read
from is named in its notes.

Everything above is about one design, and we chose that design because the theory
names it. At $(\mu,s,a,r,d_Z)=(2,3,\tfrac34,\tfrac83,3)$ the frontier holds at
$\kappa\alpha=0.2560$ against its threshold of $\tfrac14$, a margin of $0.0060$,
and the leading Step-4 product accordingly climbs from $11.72$ to $46.74$ across
the grid at $c_\delta=1$ (\cref{tab:sim-limitlaw}, Panel B). What the experiment
measured was therefore the remainder, in a design where the remainder was always
going to dominate. Whether the limit law binds anywhere a reader can reach is a
different question, and nothing above answers it.

We answer it by rerunning the same estimator at a configuration with room to
spare. Design H is $(\mu,s,a,r,d_Z,p_K)=(5,4,\tfrac25,\tfrac{21}{8},1,8)$ at
$p=2$, which gives $\kappa\alpha=0.3818$ against the same threshold and a
frontier margin of $0.1318$, more than twenty times the shipped one. Neither the
estimator nor the replication path is touched; what changes is the configuration
and the two laws drawn from it, DGP-HA and DGP-HB. The configuration clears the
ten conditions the shipped one clears, which is what \cref{tab:supp-h-design}
sets side by side; both laws are validated at the same moment conditions (\cref{tab:supp-h-dgpvalid}), and the operator each realises is recorded beside them (\cref{tab:supp-h-spectrum}).

The headroom is bought from the smoothness index $\mu$ and not from the
propensity score. Design H runs $r=2.625$ against the shipped $2.667$, so its
propensity is no smoother than the one already in hand, and the reason is A5(i).
That condition sets $\hat\delta_n$ to the larger of a propensity branch and a
parametric branch of order $n^{-1/2}\sqrt{\ln n}$, so raising $\alpha$ pushes the
propensity branch under a floor, below which $\alpha$ stops mattering. The floor
binds at every cell of Design H and at no cell of the shipped design, which the
ledger records in its own branch column (\cref{tab:supp-h-budget}).

What the experiment turns on is the realised budget. At $c_\delta=0.25$ it runs
from $0.635$ at $n=125$ up to $0.721$ at $n=1{,}000$ and then down to $0.397$, so
it is below one at every cell of both laws and falling across the part of the
grid where the samples are large. At $c_\delta=0.35$ it crosses below one at
$n=64{,}000$ and reaches $0.778$. The shipped arm at the smaller of its two
constants runs from $0.73$ to $2.92$ and rises throughout
(\cref{tab:sim-limitlaw}, Panels A and C; \cref{fig:sim-h-budget} draws both
designs). That contrast is the experiment: a remainder present but below budget,
which is a stronger test than the exact-nuisance ablation of
\cref{tab:sim-ablation} and one the shipped grid could not run.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{../figures/sim/sim_thm_rootn_headroom_budget.pdf}
\caption{The remainder budget at the two designs}
\label{fig:sim-h-budget}
\begin{minipage}{\textwidth}\footnotesize
\textit{Notes:} The leading Step-4 product $\sqrt n\,\delta_n^{2}$ at the two
configurations. It is a deterministic function of the design, so no Monte Carlo
standard error attaches to any point drawn. Both axes are logarithmic. The
horizontal line at one separates remainders the $\sqrt n$ statement can absorb
from those it cannot, so a series below that line at a given $n$ marks a cell in
which A5(ii) holds at the realised size of the nuisance error. Panels are the two
configurations: Design H, $(\mu,s,a,r,d_Z,p_K)=(5,4,\tfrac25,\tfrac{21}{8},1,8)$
at $p=2$, and the design of the preceding pages, $(2,3,\tfrac34,\tfrac83,3,8)$ at
$p=4$. The three series are the three values of $c_\delta$, the constant in the
$O_P(\delta_n)$ of A5(ii), which scales the product quadratically. Design H turns
over at $n=1{,}000$ and falls thereafter at all three constants, while the
shipped design rises at all three across the whole range; that difference in
direction, and not the level of either, is what the figure carries. The levels
are \cref{tab:supp-h-budget} for Design H and \cref{tab:sim-limitlaw} for the
shipped design. Source:
\texttt{scripts/simulations/sim\_thm\_rootn\_headroom.R}; figure
\texttt{paper/figures/sim/sim\_thm\_rootn\_headroom\_budget.pdf}.
\end{minipage}
\end{figure}

We fixed the decision rule before the run and we state it in the form it was
written. Nominal coverage within two Monte Carlo standard errors, at cells whose
realised budget is below one, confirms the limit law at a feasible $n$ and scopes
the verdict above to the shipped design; coverage off nominal at those cells
exhausts the remainder explanation and implicates the theorem, the variance
estimator or the implementation; and no admissible law with a budget below one at
a feasible $n$ would itself have been the finding, with the binding constraint
named.

The criterion is met at $21$ of the $23$ cells the table prints, and both of the
misses are at the smallest sample size on the grid (\cref{tab:sim-h-verdict}). At
$n=125$ coverage is
$0.940$ in both laws and $2.98$ standard errors below nominal in each, the two
laws agreeing to every digit printed. At every $n\ge354$ coverage is inside the
bar in both laws, at a budget below one. The outcome is ordered by the sample
size and not by the law: on the criterion fixed above, and with the remainder
present and priced, the estimator matches its limit law from $n=354$ upward and
at $n=125$ it does not. That threshold is a threshold on $95\%$ coverage and on
nothing else; the standard-deviation ratio reaches the same bar at a larger
sample size, which we give below.

\emph{We read the experiment as confirming \cref{thm:rootn} at a feasible sample
size}, and the qualification the section opened with is carried into that
reading: Design H runs the same zero anchor and was not put through the
population check that settles N1 on the two laws of the preceding pages, so
whether this confirmation sits inside the N1 clause of (T-2) is not
established. The two misses are
recorded and not set aside, and the reason they do not
overturn that reading is a property of the budget rather than a judgement about
them: below one is not the same as small, and at $n=125$ the budget falls below
one through $\sqrt n$ rather than through $\delta_n$. We give that argument, and
the statistic that orders the misses across both designs and both constants, in
the closing paragraphs of this section rather than here.

The measure the shipped verdict failed on is the ratio of the simulated standard
deviation to its asymptotic value, and it is where the two designs separate. At
matched sample size and matched constant $c_\delta=0.25$ the
shipped design sits $5.83$, $4.93$, $3.09$ and $3.37$ standard errors from its
target at $n=1{,}000$ through $n=22{,}627$ (\cref{tab:sim-seunits}), while Design
H sits at $2.12$,
$1.74$, $0.61$ and $0.18$ (\cref{tab:supp-h-seunits}); over those four cells
the budget runs from $1.27$ to
$2.22$ and rises in the first case (\cref{tab:sim-limitlaw}, Panel A), and from
$0.721$ to $0.556$ and falls in the
second (\cref{tab:supp-h-budget}). Design H clears the two-standard-error bar on that ratio in both laws at
that constant from $n=8{,}000$ upward, at $0.61$ and $0.51$, and misses it in at
least one law at every smaller sample size, at $6.35$ and $7.35$ as late as
$n=354$. The sample size at which this design's limit law becomes accurate is
therefore $n=354$ on coverage and $n=8{,}000$ on scale, and we carry both
numbers rather than the smaller one alone. Both designs clear the bar at
$n=181{,}019$ and both miss it at $n=125$, and the second of those needs saying.

We read the two failures as a defect in the criterion and not as evidence against
\cref{thm:rootn}. The budget $\sqrt n\,\delta_n^{2}$ is a product, and at $n=125$
it falls below one through $\sqrt n$ and not through $\delta_n$: the realised
$\delta_n$ there is $0.2384$ at $c_\delta=0.25$ (\cref{tab:supp-h-budget})
against a $\|\vdagger\|$ of $0.7071$, so the nuisance error is about a third of
the object being estimated and no premise of the theorem is close to holding. The
statistic that does order the failures is the realised linearisation residual,
and it orders them across both designs and both constants. It is $1.015$ at the
shipped design's $n=125$ cell (\cref{tab:sim-limitlaw}, Panel A) and $0.611$ and
$1.029$ at Design H's two (\cref{tab:supp-h-limitlaw}); all three have a budget
below one and all three miss. It is $0.265$ at Design H's $n=181{,}019$ cell at
$c_\delta=1$, whose budget is $6.350$, and that cell misses nothing.

That last cell is the converse case and it carries as much of the point as the
failures do. Its budget is more than six times the bar and the largest of its
five measures is $1.63$ standard errors (\cref{tab:supp-h-seunits}). A budget
above one does not predict a miss and a budget below one does not predict a
match; what predicts both is the size of the remainder the estimator realises.

Eight cells inside the passing range depart on the wider battery, and we flag
them rather than absorb them: all eight carry an ``outside 2 SE'' whole-battery
verdict at $n\ge354$ in \cref{tab:sim-h-verdict}, at five of them the largest of
the five measures is the standard-deviation ratio of the preceding paragraphs,
and at the other three it is the worst studentised quantile, at $2.58$, $3.28$
and $2.19$. The largest of the three needs its own reading. At DGP-HA,
$c_\delta=0.25$ and $n=64{,}000$, the largest quantile gap is $3.28$
standard errors while $95\%$ coverage is exactly nominal at $z=0.00$, the
standard-deviation ratio is $0.22$ and the centring is $2.49$. That gap sits at
the median while the four tail quantiles are inside a quarter of a standard
error, a reading taken from the run object and not from \cref{tab:supp-h-quantiles}, which prints eight cells and not this one. So the two measures that
move at that cell are location measures and the two that do not are scale
measures, and the cells on either side of it, at $n=22{,}627$ and
$n=181{,}019$, are clean on all five. \cref{tab:supp-h-seunits} reports five
measures at each of $48$ cells, and a two-standard-error bar is expected to be
crossed about once in twenty comparisons. We report the cells; we do not claim
they are nothing.

Two of the caveats above carry over unchanged. The realised operator is again
more ill-posed than H1 admits, its fitted power index running to $8.252$ and
$8.516$ against the $0.400$ of the design (\cref{tab:supp-h-spectrum}), and no
law violating an assumption is run here either, so a match remains a
non-rejection. The studentised quantiles at $n=1{,}000$ and $n=181{,}019$, in
both laws and at both of the extreme constants, are drawn in \cref{fig:supp-h-qq}; the largest quantile gap among those eight cells is $2.15$ standard
errors. \cref{tab:supp-h-quantiles} prints the same statistic cell by cell at $n=22{,}627$ and
$n=181{,}019$, where the largest is $2.29$.

We separate what this settles from what it does not. It settles that the verdict
of the preceding pages is a statement about the shipped design and not about
\cref{thm:rootn}: at a frontier margin of $0.1318$ the pre-committed criterion is
met from $n=354$ upward, and at the matched constant $c_\delta=0.25$
the standard-deviation ratio clears its bar from $n=8{,}000$, while the same
estimator, run from the same code, does not clear that ratio until $n=181{,}019$
when the margin is $0.0060$. It does not settle that the limit law binds at every
admissible constant. Design H clears the budget nowhere on this grid at
$c_\delta=1$, and the parametric branch of A5(i) binds at each of its cells, so
what puts the budget below one here is the constant and not the configuration;
$c_\delta$ is not identified, and the two values remain as
equally admissible as they were above. Of the three readings we offered an
applied reader above, the second is therefore a statement about the shipped
design, and so is the under-coverage the third opens with: at every cell of
Panel A with $n\ge354$ Design H's nominal $90\%$ coverage is inside the same
two-standard-error bar in both laws, and it sits above nominal at four of them:
DGP-HA's $n=1{,}000$ at $+0.81$, and DGP-HB's $n=2{,}828$, $n=64{,}000$ and
$n=181{,}019$ at $+0.38$, $+1.86$ and $+0.43$, with DGP-HB's $n=8{,}000$ exactly
at nominal (\cref{tab:supp-h-seunits}). None of the four clears a
two-standard-error bar. The
first stands as written at $\mathsf L=2$, which is the cardinality both designs
run; the section on cardinality below is where that qualifier is earned. So does the third's
closing clause, which turns on whether a reader's own configuration clears
\eqref{eq:frontier} and not on the coverage record of any one design.

\section*{Monte Carlo: the instrument's cardinality}

This section is the third of the article's four Monte Carlo experiments, which
varies the instrument's cardinality on the design of the two sections above and
holds everything else fixed. It adds no result: the text is the article's, moved
here unchanged except for the cross-references a move breaks.
Everything above runs at $\mathsf L=2$, and we now vary the one thing the two
designs held fixed. \Cref{thm:rootn} is stated at general finite $\mathsf L$, so
a reader entitled to the four-cell instrument of Section 6 of the article is
entitled to ask
whether the limit law is as accurate there. This arm runs the shipped design's
own configuration, $(\mu,s,a,\alpha)=(2,3,\tfrac34,0.32)$ at $p=4$ and $d_Z=3$,
at $\mathsf L\in\{2,4\}$ and $n\in\{1{,}000,8{,}000,64{,}000\}$, with $5{,}000$
replications in every cell.

One factor varies. The three rate constants, the injection regime, the $n$ grid,
the replication count and the overlap floor are identical across the two panels,
and the leading Step-4 product $\sqrt n\,\delta_n^{2}$ is $1.27$, $1.88$ and
$2.56$ in both, so nothing the remainder accounting prices differs between them
(\cref{tab:sim-card}). The binary panel is the estimator of the preceding pages
and not a re-implementation of it: thirty-six objects are bit-identical against
the pre-cardinality sources, from the configuration symbols through the
population objects to a whole replication (\cref{tab:sim-l2identity}). That
identity holds at the object level and at one replication and not at a cell mean:
the cardinality arm draws its own stream, so its Panel A and Panel A of
\cref{tab:sim-limitlaw} are distinct $5{,}000$-replication realisations of one
design rather than the same numbers printed twice. At the three sample sizes they
share they differ by at most $1.6$ Monte Carlo standard errors of the difference
on every statistic that carries one, worst at the standard-deviation ratio at
$n=1{,}000$.

The two panels do not agree. At $\mathsf L=2$ the linearisation residual that
\eqref{eq:rootn} sends to zero falls $0.657\to0.474\to0.363$ and $95\%$ coverage
is $0.946$, $0.950$ and $0.948$. At $\mathsf L=4$ the same residual \emph{rises},
$0.856\to0.909\to1.230$, and coverage decays $0.941\to0.925\to0.895$. At
$n=64{,}000$ the worst of the five measures is $2.20$ standard errors at
$\mathsf L=2$ and $18.91$ at $\mathsf L=4$, and the four-cell entry grows
monotonically across the grid while the binary one falls
(\cref{tab:sim-card-se}). The studentised quantiles carry the same shape: at
$\mathsf L=4$ and $n=64{,}000$ the $0.95$ quantile is $2.042$ against the
normal's $1.645$, a gap of $13.29$ standard errors, while no quantile at
$\mathsf L=2$ departs by more than $2.20$ anywhere on the grid
(\cref{tab:sim-card-q}; \cref{fig:sim-card-qq} draws them).

\emph{We read this as \cref{prp:orthog}(iii) confirmed rather than \cref{thm:rootn}
refuted}, and the reason is that the two panels differ in the condition the
proposition names and in nothing else the remainder accounting prices. By
\cref{cor:centarity} N1 is $p(\mathsf L-1)$ scalar conditions and not $p$, which
at the $p=4$ of this design is four conditions at $\mathsf L=2$ and twelve at
$\mathsf L=4$. The design satisfies the four and violates the twelve. Computed in
population rather than estimated, the largest entrywise defect
$\max_{j,l}\|E[L_\star\mid\Delta Z]_{jl}\|$ is $8.23\times10^{-6}$ against a
$\|L_\star\|$ of $2.4613$ at $\mathsf L=2$, and $0.7293$ against $3.8227$ at
$\mathsf L=4$, so the ratio moves from $3.3\times10^{-6}$ to $0.191$
(\cref{tab:sim-n1defect}).

The identity at $\mathsf L=2$ is structural and not a small number. All of the
solved representer's coefficient energy sits on odd $q$ there, where $A_q$ is odd
in $u$, so $L_\star$ is odd in $u$; $\Delta U$ is independent of $(\Delta Z,W)$
by construction and symmetric about zero; and the conditional mean vanishes by
parity. The share of that energy sitting on odd $q$ is $1.000000$ at
$\mathsf L=2$ against $0.707$ at $\mathsf L=4$, so the mechanism is measured and
not inferred from the defect it produces, and the residual $3.3\times10^{-6}$ is
the antiderivative grid's own parity error rather than a live entry. DGP-B
repeats the pattern at both cardinalities, so this is a property of the
construction and not of one law.

\Cref{prp:orthog}(iii) makes N1 necessary \emph{and sufficient} for the moment's
$\varrho$-derivative to vanish, and the two panels exhibit both directions. Under
N1 the first-order propensity term
$\sqrt n\,\mathbb E_n[L_\star(\hat\varrho-\varrho)]$ is a centred average of
quantities of size $r_n$ and decays at $n^{-\alpha}=n^{-0.320}$; when N1 fails,
that term carries a non-vanishing mean and grows at $n^{1/2-\alpha}=n^{+0.180}$.
Both references are read off the design rather than fitted. Measured, the term
decays at $n^{-0.302}$ where the condition holds, which is $1.4$ Monte Carlo
standard errors from the orthogonality reference, and grows at $n^{+0.206}$ where
it fails, which is $2.0$ from the failure reference, at a standard error of
$0.013$ on each exponent (Panel E of \cref{tab:sim-n1defect}). \emph{The condition
holds where the proposition requires the term to decay and fails where it
requires the term to grow.} At $\mathsf L=2$ the term decays at the predicted
rate. At $\mathsf L=4$ it grows, which is the direction N1's failure forces and
the one a centred average cannot produce; the $+0.206$ sits two standard errors
above the failure reference rather than on it, and we do not read it as that
reference recovered. Under N1 failure $T_2$ carries a growing mean term beside a
still-live centred one, whose size Panel E prices at $\Lambda\tau_n=0.1813$
against a total of $0.8225$ at $n=8{,}000$, so a slope over a single leg is a
weighted average of two exponents and bounds the mean term's exponent from below
rather than measuring it.

Those are not the exponents \cref{tab:sim-ablsplit-channel} implies, and the
difference is a confound in that arm's measurement code, which we removed rather
than absorbed. The arm forms its propensity residual against $\Delta U-\Delta h$
and evaluates $L_\star$ at that residual, so the $T_2$ it accumulates carries the
$\sqrt n\,\|h\|r_n$ cross-product the theorem prices separately: a contamination
free of $\mathsf L$, carrying a non-zero conditional mean, negligible beside a
live defect and dominant where the defect is absent. Its levels fall
$0.337\to0.270$ at $\mathsf L=2$ and rise $0.569\to0.843$ at $\mathsf L=4$, which
are slopes of $-0.108$ and $+0.189$ over the leg, and those are the figures that
table prints. Re-running the $T_2$ accumulation alone with $h$ switched off, at
$1{,}500$ replications on a separate stream whose $h$-on rows reproduce the
shipped ones to within $2.1$ standard errors of the difference, moves
$\mathsf L=2$ from $-0.100$ to $-0.302$ and $\mathsf L=4$ from $+0.154$ to
$+0.206$. The binary arm sits $17$
standard errors from the orthogonality reference with $h$ on and $1.4$ from it
with $h$ off, so removing the confound dissolves the binary anomaly. It does not
sharpen the four-cell one: $+0.154$ and $+0.206$ are both $0.026$ from the
failure reference, so the estimate crosses that reference rather than closing on
it, and it crosses to the side the preceding paragraph reads as a bound.

Each exponent is still a slope over one leg, $n=1{,}000$ to $8{,}000$, and one
leg shows no curvature. What has changed is where the legs land: both now sit on
their own reference rather than between the two, and the discrepancy a third
sample size was going to adjudicate has been answered instead by switching off
the term that produced it. A third point would buy a check on curvature and we
did not run one, for the reason the closing paragraphs of this section give.

The ablation localises the failure to one nuisance and exonerates the other
twice. Two arms switch on exactly one estimated nuisance each, at
$n\in\{1{,}000,8{,}000\}$ and $5{,}000$ replications. The $\hat\varrho$ arm
reaches $12.10$ standard errors at $\mathsf L=4$ and rises, while converging at
$\mathsf L=2$ at $2.97$ and falling; its residual at four cells is $0.874$ and
$0.913$, which reproduces the full arm's $0.856$ and $0.909$ to within $2.2$ and
$0.4$ per cent, both computed on the unrounded values and not on the four digits
printed, so switching that one nuisance on reproduces the whole failure. The
$\hat\ell$ arm's residual decays at $-0.171$ at $\mathsf L=2$ and $-0.172$ at
$\mathsf L=4$, the same exponent to a thousandth, which is what ``the cardinality
is not the problem in this channel'' looks like (\cref{tab:sim-ablsplit}). A5(iv)
is exonerated a second time by a measurement and not by an arm: the norm the
moment consumes divided by the norm A5(iv) prices is $0.463$ at $\mathsf L=2$
against $0.420$ at $\mathsf L=4$, so the Frobenius bound is \emph{conservative} at the
higher cardinality rather than slack there, and the measurement moves the wrong
way for any account that blames it.

One entry of that ablation does not fall and we flag it rather than absorb it.
The $\hat\ell$ arm's worst of five at $\mathsf L=4$ goes only from $6.49$ to
$5.03$, against $6.29$ to $1.75$ at $\mathsf L=2$, and at $n=8{,}000$ the
statistic carrying it is the centring and not the scale. The residual
\eqref{eq:rootn} names decays there at the binary arm's own exponent, so the
locating claim stands; what does not stand is a reading of that arm as clean on
every measure.

The design remains admissible at both cardinalities and the deterioration is not
a boundary artefact. Overlap clears its floor at four cells, at
$\lambda_{\min}(\Omega)=0.0273$ against $\varepsilon_\varrho/\mathsf L=0.0250$;
the Jacobian's condition number is $3.63$ against $3.62$; and the balancing
residual A2 asks for is $3.6\times10^{-5}$ against $4.2\times10^{-7}$, which the
remainder accounting prices at $1.9\times10^{-4}$ against a leading product of
$2.56$ (\cref{tab:sim-card-design}). What does move with the cardinality is the
budget (R-a) prices, $\sup|\ell_\star|$ rising from $3.04$ to $7.56$.

Two limits. The four-cell grid stops at $n=64{,}000$ and the ablation at
$n=8{,}000$, in both cases on cost: one replication at $\mathsf L=4$ and
$n=64{,}000$ takes $2.20$ seconds, so a cell of $5{,}000$ of them is three hours
of processor time and a little under twenty-three minutes on the eight workers
the run distributes it over, and we would rather carry two well-separated points at
$5{,}000$ replications than three at a thinned count. And the arm injects its nuisances at fixed rate
constants, so it prices a remainder of a declared size and establishes nothing
about whether any estimator attains that size.

What this changes above is the first of the three readings, and only its last
clause. The remainder accounting is complete for nuisance errors of the priced
size at $\mathsf L=2$ and is not at $\mathsf L=4$, because the term it completes
is the one N1 deletes at the first cardinality and leaves standing at the second.
Section 6 of the article runs at $\mathsf L=4$ and reports
what the same defect measures on its own data, where at $n=983$ it is not
resolvable from zero.

\section*{Monte Carlo: the shipped engine on three designs}

This section is the fourth of the article's four Monte Carlo experiments, the
one the article still prints. Three of its floats stay there: the balanced
design at three cardinalities is Table 1 of the article, the misspecified
propensity is Table 2 of the article, and the record of when the stopping rule
fires is Table 3 of the article. What follows is the rest of the experiment: the
argument that the three suites do not merge, the three blocks set side by side,
N1 measured at the weight the engine solves for, the skewed design, the
interval's scale, and the paired cardinality contrast, together with the
article's full text for the experiment. It adds no result.
Both experiments above run the theory's own sieve construction against population
objects computed in closed form, and both draw their nuisances as the truth plus
an error of controlled size rather than estimating them. Section 6 runs neither.
A third suite closes that gap: a multinomial design estimated by the shipped
engine, the same code Section 6 estimates with, with every nuisance fitted from
the sample and the instrument read at $\mathsf L\in\{2,3,4\}$ off one draw.

One departure of that engine from the theory it implements has since been
repaired, and we state the repair here with what it is worth measured rather
than asserted. The measurements of this paragraph are printed in Panels B and D
of \cref{tab:supp-bdrylayer}. C3(ii) asks the boundary kernel for vanishing
truncated moments at every order $0\le j\le p_K-1$, and the family
\cref{lem:bdryfam} constructs delivers all of them; the engine used to renormalise to unit mass at each design point,
which realises the $j=0$ member alone, and it now runs that family at $p_K=8$,
which is the kernel Section 6 estimates with. Both configurations were run, and
each lands on the exponent its own construction predicts. The renormalised
kernel converges to $1.003$, the degraded $h_x^{1}$ that enforcing the zeroth
moment and nothing higher buys; the family converges to $7.984$, which is
$h_x^{p_K}=h_x^{8}$, because $\vdagger$ is $C^\infty$ on this design and
\eqref{eq:truncmom} kills the orders $j=1,\dots,7$. The guarantee \eqref{eq:xsmoothbias} carries
is $h_x^{s-1/2}=h_x^{2.5}$, and the two exponents bracket it: the first
fails it and the second clears it.

Two things moved together, and the second is a bandwidth. The $x$-bandwidth is
now $h_x=n^{-0.40}$, the midpoint of the window $(0.360,0.440)$, and the
boundary layer stopped swallowing the design. Within three bandwidths of an
endpoint sat every pooled design point at every $n$ up to $2{,}828$ before, and
$99.41$ down to $51.93$ per cent at the four sample sizes above that; after, the
share is $48.55$ per cent at $n=500$ and $4.22$ at $n=181{,}019$
(\cref{tab:supp-bdrylayer}, Panel A). The same measurement returns $884$ of the
$1{,}966$ pooled design points of Section 6's panel, which the notes to \cref{tab:supp-app-bdrymom} record, and that is $44.96$ per cent.
The bias that enters one hypothesis, (P-g), read as an upper bound on $h_x$, is
where the two changes are visible together. Its realised ratio used to
\emph{climb} across the grid, from $3.13$ at $n=125$ to $8.09$ at
$n=181{,}019$, where the hypothesis asks for $O(1)$; it now falls to a plateau
of about $9.6\times10^{-7}$, moving by $-0.0406$ in log-log terms over the last
four sample sizes at a level spread of $13.4$ per cent. \emph{We report a plateau and
not a fitted rate.} A log-log line through the whole grid returns $-0.813$, and
it is the wrong model for a curve that falls by a factor of $328$ and then
flattens; its regression standard error is $175$ times the Monte Carlo one,
which is the diagnostic that says so; that ratio is taken on the unrounded
standard errors, which the panel's three digits round to $173$. Under the renormalised arm the window
(P-g) left against C5$'$(ii) was non-empty but narrow, clearing by $0.061$ at
the frontier-clearing $\alpha=0.32$ and by $0.006$ at $\alpha=3/8$, which
\cref{rem:h6bandwidth} already declares an illustration rather than an
admissible design.

The cap moves with the repair, and the move corrects two constants rather than
adding a fresh distortion. In the old configuration $c_C$
was carrying a compact-support half-width retired with the kernel it belonged
to, and $\mathsf c_2$ was the interior kernel's maximum where C3(ii) asks for
the sup of the envelope. \emph{Correcting them is not the same as making the cap
tight}: \eqref{eq:cap} still
exceeds $\hat\delta_n^{-2}$ by $7.32\times10^{8}$ to $2.78\times10^{9}$ through
the over-normalisation $\omega_n/\|\hat{\mathcal A}\|$ that Panel C prices, and
nothing below touches that. Correcting both, at $n=500$ the cap \eqref{eq:cap} moves by a factor
of $344{,}503$, of which the constants carry $89{,}741$, the bandwidth $3.47$
and the kernel family exactly $1.00$. The constants leg is
$0.1551\times34.039^{4}$ against the retired $4.0\times0.8727^{4}$; the
bandwidth enters \eqref{eq:cap} as $h_x^{-1}$ and nothing else, so its leg is
the ratio $0.2885/0.0833$ of the two bandwidths as the exponent moves from
$n^{-0.20}$ to $n^{-0.40}$, taken on the unrounded bandwidths and not on the four
digits printed, which give $3.46$. What the three derived legs leave over is the
realised $h_u$ coupling, $1.108$ at $n=500$ and $1.054$ and $1.027$ at
$n=2{,}000$ and $8{,}000$, and it is reported as a residual so that it cannot
absorb an arithmetic slip. \emph{The family contributes exactly $1.00$.} $\Theta_I$
enters \eqref{eq:cap} through $c_C$ and $\mathsf c_2$ alone, so the boundary
family is free in the cap and is paid for in the bias, which is where it should
be paid. The post-repair values, at $n=500$, $2{,}000$ and $8{,}000$, are
$\omega_n=27{,}200.1$, $37{,}777.9$ and $52{,}744.8$, and
$\bar m_n=3.95\times10^{10}$, $1.85\times10^{11}$ and $8.76\times10^{11}$, at
$\mathsf c_2=34.039$ and $c_C=0.1551$ (\cref{tab:sim-stopping}, Panel C$'$).

\emph{We have priced the two exponents against the $x$-smoothing bias and against
(P-g) and nowhere else}: neither is traced through the sieve entropy bound,
through A5(vi$'$), or through \cref{thm:rootn}'s reading of $\delta_n$ off
A5(ii), and if either reaches any of those three the accounting just given is
incomplete. The gap was between the theory and the implementation and never
inside the theory, which is why C3(ii) is stated at every order and why closing
it cost a kernel and not a hypothesis.

\emph{It also cost draws, and we price that here rather than in the notes to the
tables that pay it.} A kernel that kills the truncated moments of every order
$1\le j\le p_K-1$ cannot be non-negative, so $\hat\pi$ under the boundary family
is a higher-order density estimate and can take a non-positive value at a design
point. The adjoint divides by $\hat\pi$, so the engine refuses to build the
operator and the replication is dropped rather than returned degraded. \emph{What
fails is the sample reference density and not a hypothesis.} The adjoint of
Section 3 of the article carries the population $\pi$, and the article states no condition on
the estimate that stands in for it, so we name the object rather than an
assumption tag. It is the same failure that leaves the estimator infeasible in
the $\mu$g/m$^3$ coordinate of Section 6, where Panel C of \cref{tab:app-phi}
prints it in those words; it is reached there through a rescaled coordinate and
here through a small design set.

The mechanism is that design set together with the cross-fitting geometry, and
neither of the two alone. Every loss across the four arms of this suite falls
where the operator is built on a cross-fitting fold of $160$, $320$ or $640$
points, which is $\lceil0.4n\rceil$ at $n=400$, $800$ and $1{,}600$, and the count
falls as the fold grows. No operator built on a whole draw has tripped the guard,
neither at the $400$ points and more the uncross-fitted arms hand it nor at the
$160$ of $60$ fresh balanced draws taken at the smallest fold size. \emph{The two
counts are on different scales and the second is not a threshold in the first}:
what separates the arms that lose draws is that a cross-fitted operator builds
$\hat\pi$ on a subsample while the support it is evaluated over still comes from
the whole draw. The multinomial $\varphi$-step
arm, which is not the $36$-cell arm of the limit-law section above, builds its operator on
the whole draw and keeps all $24$ of its paths in each of its twenty-seven cells,
which is what the bracketed denominators of Table 3 of the article
record; its plug-in companion, also on the whole draw, keeps all $504$ of its
replications, a count printed in no table and read off
\texttt{quality\_reports/sim/sim\_multinomial\_phiplugin.rds}; the arms that
partition into $\mathsf F=5$ folds, of which the tables below are one, hand the
operator $160$ points at $n=400$ and lose between none and eight draws per cell,
most of them there. What is lost does not depend on the cardinality, which is
what the three tables below record when their headers print the count as equal
at all $\mathsf L$, and what leaves the paired contrast defined. The realised
counts are stated with the precision statement they govern below.

\emph{The three suites do not merge into a single cardinality contrast, and we say so
before setting them beside each other.} They differ in the design, in the
estimator and in the nuisance regime, and their sample-size grids do not
intersect at any point: the first two run $125$ to $181{,}019$ and the third runs
$400$, $800$ and $1{,}600$. A table whose columns read $\mathsf L=2$ and
$\mathsf L=4$ but whose rows come from two of them would attribute three
differences to the cardinality. Every table in this section therefore obeys one
rule, carried in the panel headers rather than in the notes so that a reader who
reads only the body still cannot merge two blocks by accident: \emph{one row is one
design, one estimator and one nuisance regime, and the cardinality varies within a
row and never across one} (\cref{tab:sim-merged-designs}).

One precision statement governs the third suite at rates near nominal, and it
does not govern the rest of it. The suite was run at $120$ replications and
returns between $112$ and $120$ usable ones, for the reason given above. The
count is a property of the cell and not of the cardinality: it is identical
across $\mathsf L=2$, $3$ and $4$ in all nine cells, which is what leaves the
paired contrast defined, and it is lowest at the misspecified design at $n=400$.
At a coverage rate of $0.95$ the Monte Carlo standard error is about $0.02$, and
two of them resolve to $\pm0.040$ at the fullest cell and $\pm0.041$ at the
thinnest, so a gap smaller than that is not evidence of anything. \emph{That is the
smallest resolution in the suite, and it is calibrated at one point.} The
standard error grows as coverage moves toward a half, and at the misspecified
constant, where coverage runs from $0.277$ to $0.795$, the standard errors the
table prints are $0.038$ to $0.046$; two of those are $\pm0.076$ to $\pm0.092$,
about twice the figure just quoted. Every reading below is therefore priced at
the standard error its own cell prints. The paired contrasts are the
sharper instrument, because the three cardinalities run on the same draw and the
same partition, so the difference carries its own standard error rather than the
sum of two (\cref{tab:sim-merged-precision}), and the claims below rest on those.

\emph{What the dropped draws could have done is bounded and no longer merely
disclosed.} A cell drawn at $B=120$ and used at $b$ has its coverage inside
$[\hat p\,b/B,\ \hat p\,b/B+(B-b)/B]$ whatever the missing draws would have
returned, and each of the three tables now carries that bound in its own header
rather than in its notes: at most $0.024$ on the balanced design, $0.032$ on the
skewed one and $0.063$ on the misspecified one; at $n=1{,}600$ it is at most
$0.008$, which is under the smallest coverage standard error the three tables
print at that sample size, $0.014$. \emph{That comparison is against the coverage
standard errors of Panel C and against no other column}: Panel A's bias standard
errors at the same sample size run down to $0.0053$, and the bound does not
govern a bias. Readings below taken at $n=400$ and $n=800$ carry the
larger figure rather than that one.
The selection is real and its direction is known, a draw surviving when the
nonparametric stage behaved, so the printed rates are the optimistic reading of
that interval.

One hypothesis of \cref{thm:rootn} had been computed on no multinomial design,
and computing it here returns a failure. N1 asks that
$E[L(\Delta U,\Delta Z)\mid\Delta Z]$ vanish, which \cref{cor:centarity} types
as $p(\mathsf L-1)$ scalar conditions, and it is the clause the preceding
section found breaking at $\mathsf L=4$ on the design the theory names.
Measured on the weight the engine solves for, and reported as the entrywise
defect over $\max_{j,l}\|L_{jl}\|$, which is that section's own statistic to
the digit, it runs from $0.531$ to $0.720$ across the nine
design-by-cardinality cells at $n_{\mathrm{solve}}=640$
(\cref{tab:sim-multinomial-n1defect}, Panel A). The weight is solved at the true
propensity and the true residual, so what is measured is the weight class and not
the two nuisance errors (T-3) and (T-4) price separately; on the misspecified
design that means its own true propensity, and its row is a third design rather
than a statement about the misspecification. Block I returns
$3.3\times10^{-6}$ at $\mathsf L=2$ and $0.191$ at $\mathsf L=4$ against the
same denominator. \emph{N1 fails on all three designs at all three cardinalities},
and the spread across $\mathsf L$ within a design is at most $0.088$ where the
level is $0.53$ to $0.72$.

We give three certificates for that reading, because a negative result about a
quantity whose null value is zero is worth more measured against a floor than
asserted. The computation is closed form rather than estimated: the design draws
$\Delta U$ conditionally on $\Delta Z=z$ as a normal whose mean and whose
variance both move with $z$, so the inner expectation is a normal integral taken
at machine precision and the routine reads no $z$-sample. Redrawn with that
dependence switched off, which leaves $\Delta U$ independent of $\Delta Z$, the
same code returns $5.4\times10^{-15}$ to $7.6\times10^{-14}$ over its $72$
draws, and the smallest live ratio anywhere in the arm, $0.3145$, sits $12.6$
orders of magnitude above that floor. Nor does the defect shrink: across the
three solve folds the arm realises,
$n_{\mathrm{solve}}\in\{160,320,640\}$, the log-log slope runs $-0.133$ to
$+0.064$, where a sampling error would fall and a restriction on the weight
class does not (Panel B). And an independent quadrature route agrees with the
closed form to at most $1.7\times10^{-4}$ at every printed cell, against
quantities of size $23$ to $60$, and to $1.4\times10^{-5}$ in relative terms at
the worst of the $324$ live solve draws (Panel C).

\emph{This is not a defect in \cref{thm:rootn} and we do not report it as one.} It
sits between the theory and the implementation, and it is the same species as
the C3(ii) gap the opening of this section prices.
\texttt{solve\_balance\_weight} builds $\ell$ in a function class over the
residual alone, so $\Lambda$ carries no $z$ argument, and
\texttt{crossfit\_once} anchors it by subtracting a constant. The conditional
laws of $\Delta U$ given $\Delta Z$ therefore form a location-scale family with
a continuum of means, and a bounded function of $u$ alone orthogonal to every
one of them is zero almost everywhere, so the zero weight is the only member of
the implemented class that satisfies N1 on this design. The supremum of the same
ratio over centred weights that are polynomials of degree at most six in the
residual is a property of the design and of no weight, and it reads $0.8615$ at
the two well-specified designs and $0.9021$ at the third, collapsing to
$8.94\times10^{-8}$ once the conditional dependence is switched off (Panel C). The re-anchoring of Section 4 of the article would restore N1 at the same $\ell$,
and \cref{rem:anchor} admits it with no
further assumption; the engine does not build it. Two things this does not
establish. It says nothing about Section 6's data, where the defect is estimated
on a panel whose conditional law is unknown and the population argument just
given has no purchase, and it does not show that the theory's own $\ell_\star$
fails N1 here.

At the two well-specified designs the cardinality does very little, and the
measurement above says why rather than leaving it unattributed: there is no
cardinality-varying N1 mechanism on this suite to produce a cardinality-varying
divergence, the defect being live at every cell and of about one size. The bias at
$n=1{,}600$ is inside two of its own Monte Carlo standard errors at all nine
cells of the balanced design and at eight of the nine skewed ones, the exception
being the skewed constant at four cells, at $-0.0138$ $(0.0053)$. The quantity
\cref{thm:rootn} makes constant in $n$, $\sqrt n$ times the standard deviation,
falls across the grid at sixteen of the eighteen cells of those two designs and
is larger at $n=1{,}600$ than at $n=400$ at two, both of them the balanced
constant, by $19.19$ and $5.35$ per cent. \emph{Neither of those two moves is resolved
from flat.} Panel B now prints a Monte Carlo standard error for that quantity,
computed from the fourth moment rather than from the Gaussian formula, the
realised kurtosis reaching $10.8$ over the suite's $81$ cells; against it the
larger of the two is $1.50$ standard errors and the smaller is $0.45$. The paired differences at $n=1{,}600$ are
inside $2.4$ of their own standard errors at every coefficient and both
cardinalities, the largest being the balanced constant at $-0.0339$ $(0.0144)$
and the skewed $z_2$ at $-0.0152$ $(0.0076)$. The first of those is $2.35$
standard errors and stands clear of the rest; the second is $2.00$ on the printed
digits, which the print cannot separate from two either way; none of the
remaining ten reaches $1.2$.

Coverage at $n=1{,}600$ sits between $0.866$ and $0.975$ at all nine balanced
cells and between $0.867$ and $0.958$ at all nine skewed ones
(Table 1 of the article, \cref{tab:sim-merged-rootn-skewed}).
\emph{That range is true and it conceals the shape of its own low end}, which is
one-sided and does not shrink. Seven of those eighteen cells sit more than two
Monte Carlo standard errors below nominal, and they are not scattered: three are
the balanced constant, at $0.882$, $0.866$ and $0.866$ down the three
cardinalities, and four are on the skewed design, its constant at two cells and
$z_2$ at all three. On the favourable design the constant at four cells runs
$0.863$, $0.842$ and $0.866$ across the three sample sizes, which is flat and
$2.7$ standard errors under nominal at the largest of them; skewed $z_2$ at four
cells moves \emph{away} from nominal as $n$ grows, at $0.948$, $0.915$ and $0.867$.

\emph{What kind of failure that is, the interval answers and the limit law does not},
and the statistic that answers it was computed all along and printed in no table.
The mean estimated standard error over the simulated standard deviation is below
one in $77$ of the $81$ cells of this suite, below $0.85$ in $42$ and below
$0.75$ in $18$ (\cref{tab:sim-merged-seratio}); the balanced constant sits
between $0.705$ and $0.805$ and does not improve across a grid spanning a factor
of four in $n$. Take the coverage a centred normal carrying that ratio would
deliver and subtract the realised coverage: the difference is inside $\pm0.070$
at all $54$ well-specified cells, at a root mean square of $0.024$. \emph{The entire
well-specified coverage shortfall is the interval's scale and not the limit
law.} On the misspecified design the same statistic runs $-0.028$ to $+0.033$ on
the slopes and $+0.030$ to $+0.511$ on the constant, which is the bias a centred
approximation sets aside by construction. A live N1 defect predicts this
shape: by \cref{prp:orthog}(iii) the moment's $\varrho$-derivative no longer
vanishes, so $\hat\varrho$ enters at first order, and where the propensity is
correctly specified it converges at $\sqrt n$ and leaves $\hat\theta$
asymptotically normal while the sandwich omits a term and is wrong by a factor
that does not shrink. \emph{We report that as consistent with the measurement and not
as demonstrated by it}, the variance correction itself not being computed here.

The third design is the one that breaks, and it breaks in the propensity. It
misspecifies $\hat\varrho$, which is the nuisance A4(iii) prices and the one the
cardinality section above isolated. Its constant's bias does not fall in $n$ at four
cells, running $-0.3040$, $-0.3242$ and $-0.3830$, and $\sqrt n$ times its
standard deviation \emph{rises}, $6.031$, $6.960$, $8.605$, where the theorem makes it
constant. That last move is $3.40$ of the standard error Panel B now prints, so
unlike the two at the balanced design it \emph{is} resolved from flat. Coverage of the constant at $n=1{,}600$ is $0.697$ at two cells, $0.294$
at three and $0.277$ at four, and the paired bias difference against the binary
arm is $-0.2287$ $(0.0226)$ and $-0.2765$ $(0.0241)$, which are $10.1$ and $11.5$
standard errors and are not a resolution artefact
(Table 2 of the article). The two slope coefficients are untouched
at $n=1{,}600$, covering between $0.891$ and $0.950$ at every cardinality. The
damage is therefore confined to the coordinate the propensity enters, and it
grows with the number of cells at the two larger sample sizes: the $n=1{,}600$
coverages just quoted fall down the three cardinalities, those at $n=800$ run
$0.771$, $0.525$, $0.424$, and the bias grows in step at both. \emph{At $n=400$ it
does not.} Coverage there runs $0.795$, $0.661$, $0.732$ and
the bias $-0.1813$, $-0.3266$, $-0.3040$, so four cells show less damage than
three on both measures. Both reversals are inside the bound
$\mathrm{SE}\le\mathrm{SE}_3+\mathrm{SE}_4$, at $0.82$ and $0.38$ of it, and
$n=400$ under this design is the thinnest cell in the suite, at $112$ usable
replications. The direction is the one the injected-nuisance ablation found,
reached here through estimated nuisances and through the code Section 6 runs
on.

One competing explanation for that rising standard deviation is removed by an arm
that already existed and had not been read. The $\varphi$-step sweep runs the
discrepancy rule at $\tau_{\mathrm{DP}}=0$, where it never fires and the returned
iterate \emph{is} the cap, so a sweep over the cap is a fixed-$m$ variant: at
$n=1{,}600$ and $\mathsf L=4$, moving $\bar m$ from $15$ to $100$ raises the
misspecified design's integrated squared error from $0.195$ to $0.488$, at Monte
Carlo standard errors of $0.010$ and $0.067$, while it lowers the balanced
design's from $0.091$ to $0.036$ and the skewed design's from $0.118$ to $0.051$.
Those six figures are read off the $(\tau_{\mathrm{DP}},\bar m)$ sweep that
\texttt{scripts/simulations/sim\_multinomial\_phistep.R} writes to
\texttt{quality\_reports/sim/sim\_multinomial\_phistep\_sweep.rds}, at
$\tau_{\mathrm{DP}}=0$ and $\bar m\in\{15,100\}$; the sweep is a run object and
not a float, which is why they carry a path here and not a cross-reference.
\emph{The cap is therefore not an independent cause}, iterating longer helping where
the propensity is right and hurting where it is wrong. The same separation is not
available on the $\theta$ side, which would need that arm re-run at a fixed
budget, and we have not run it.

The stopping rule fails in the same place and in the same direction. At the two
well-specified designs the discrepancy rule selects an iterate inside its budget
in most replications at every cardinality, at $1.000$, $0.917$ and $0.875$ on the
balanced design at $n=1{,}600$ and $1.000$, $0.792$ and $0.667$ on the skewed one.
At the misspecified design it selects one in $0.875$ of replications at two cells,
$0.250$ at three and \emph{none at all} at four (Table 3 of the article). A
rule that never fires returns the cap, which is the configuration Section 6's
bootstrap runs under and says so.

Three readings this section does not support. It does not establish that the
shipped engine and the abstract construction agree, because no cell of the third
suite shares a sample size with either of the first two, and the merged tables
print the grids rather than interpolate between them. It does not establish
that the cardinality is harmless at the well-specified designs, because $112$ to
$120$ replications cannot resolve a coverage gap below about $\pm0.04$ and the
paired contrasts bound the \emph{bias} difference rather than the coverage one. And it
does not establish that the N1 defect is what the standard-error ratio measures:
the correction that \cref{prp:orthog}(iii) implies is not computed, and the two
quantities are set beside each other rather than fitted to one another.

\emph{its bracket is the share of draws at which the constant attains it}, not
the share for the coefficient named. Panel C carries the three certificates the
text reads: the control, which switches the conditional dependence off and
returns this script's numerical floor, run at the largest fold and at the two
well-specified designs only; $R_{\max}$, the supremum of the same ratio over
centred weights polynomial of degree at most six in the residual, which is a
property of the design and of no weight; and the largest gap between the closed
form and an independent quadrature route over a cell's draws, beside the largest
scale compared. Source:
\texttt{scripts/simulations/sim\_multinomial\_n1defect.R}; table
\texttt{paper/tables/sim/sim\_multinomial\_n1defect.tex}.
\end{tablenotes}
\end{threeparttable}
\end{table}

measurement}, being a function of the left block and of a coverage already

\section*{The empirical application: supplementary material}

This section carries the material for Section 6 of the article that the article
names but does not print. It adds no result. The article's three tables and its
figure carry the
section's findings; what follows is the construction of the estimation sample,
the variables it holds, the balance and overlap the design realises, the
parametric component along the control-set ladder, the diagnostics of the
estimator that produced the article's structural function, the tuning arms, and
the three floats that moved here from Section 6 in the second OBES cut: the
iteration-cap contrast, the N1 defect over the class of constant anchors, and
$\hat\varphi$ at eleven percentiles with its bootstrap envelope.
Every table but one is produced by
\texttt{scripts/application/app\_tsp\_run\_all.R}; the exception is
\cref{tab:supp-bdrylayer}, a Monte Carlo float placed here beside the boundary
material it explains, which comes from
\texttt{scripts/simulations/sim\_thm\_rootn\_bdrylayer.R} and is reached by
neither run-all driver. The file each table is read from is
named in its notes. The sample is the Chay--Greenstone county panel,
$T=2$, first differenced, $n=983$ throughout except where a row says otherwise.

\label{tab:supp-app-sample}

rows, so it is an empty column rather than a column with gaps, and the count of

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\begin{threeparttable}
\caption{Balance of the twenty-two differenced covariates on the instrument}
\label{tab:supp-app-balance}
\footnotesize
\input{../tables/app_tsp_balance}
\begin{tablenotes}\footnotesize
\item \textit{Notes:} $n=983$. Each row regresses one differenced covariate on
$W$ alone and reports the coefficient, its robust standard error in parentheses,
its state-clustered standard error in square brackets, and the normalised
difference, the difference in means divided by the square root of the average of
the two within-group variances. Rows are grouped by the ladder rung at which the
covariate first enters. The last three rows count the covariates whose
difference is significant at $5$ per cent under each variance, and test all
twenty-two jointly. This table is not a randomisation check: $W$ is not
randomly assigned and A1 does not require it to be independent of $\Delta Z$.
What it establishes is that $W$ and $\Delta Z$ are dependent, which matters
because the estimator centres at $W-\hat\varrho(\Delta Z)$: the dependence this
table measures is exactly what $\hat\varrho$ has to capture, and a design in
which $W$ and $\Delta Z$ were independent would make the conditional and
unconditional centrings coincide. Source:
\texttt{scripts/application/app\_tsp\_01\_diagnostics.R}; table
\texttt{paper/tables/app\_tsp\_balance.tex}.
\end{tablenotes}
\end{threeparttable}

counties outside $[0.05,0.95]$ and outside $[0.10,0.90]$, and McFadden's
pseudo-$R^{2}$. A4(i) asks $\hat\varrho$ to stay away from zero and one, so a
row fails when the extremes approach them. \emph{Since 2026-08-07 this table is

set, where the first percentile of $\hat\varrho$ is $0.030$. The last two rows condition on baseline particulates, which is the
variable the designation rule thresholds; both drive the maximum to exactly one,
so overlap fails there. Source:

% puts the last glyph of the note's final token on page 31.  The two derivations
% agreeing to a hundredth of a big point is why the arithmetic below can be
% trusted without another build.
%
% MEASURED, NOT DERIVED.  pdftotext -bbox on page 31 of the 2026-08-24
% supplement.pdf gives the folio's box as 738.53--754.07bp and the note's line

%     741.52--750.32      753.48--762.28      763.50--774.51
%     778.30--786.47

% "two" the old remedy named are the two below the folio's BOTTOM edge, at
% 763.50 and 778.30, which is the symptom and not the clearance.  \footskip is
% 30.0pt, so the whole gap between the text block ending at 720.00bp and the
% folio beginning at 738.53bp IS 18.53bp, ONE AND A HALF \footnotesize LINES at
% the 12.0bp pitch these seven lines exhibit.  Any float overrunning \textheight
% by more than that reaches the running foot.  This one overran by 66.72pt,
% which is 5.6 lines.
%
% AND FOUR IS NOT THE ANSWER EITHER.  Removing four leaves the line now at
% 729.60--738.37 as the last, clearing the folio's 738.53 by 0.16bp -- one
% seventy-fifth of a \footnotesize line.  This document already has a ruling on
% margins of that order: 0.50pt at tab:supp-app-robust "is not a margin; it is
% the width of the next edit to the note."  0.16bp is a third of that.  FIVE
% lines clears by 12.12bp and is the first honest number.  Five lines out of a

ordered by how far each block
of controls is from being an outcome of house prices: an intercept alone, five
core hedonic demand shifters, those plus five demographic variables, and all
twenty-two usable controls, whose per-capita property-tax revenue is
mechanically a function of the dependent variable. Rows are the coefficients the
first three rungs share; the housing and fiscal coefficients of column (4) are
estimated but not printed. Robust standard errors in parentheses,
state-clustered standard errors in square brackets, and stars computed from the
clustered standard error, which is the one A0's failure at Air Quality Control
Region level licenses. Column (1) is a reference point and not an estimate: its
standard error is two failed cross-fitting partitions, as
\cref{tab:supp-app-diag} shows. The object of the article's Section 6 is the
structural function and not $\theta$, so this table is a sensitivity axis
rather than a headline. $^{*}$ $p<0.10$, $^{**}$ $p<0.05$, $^{***}$ $p<0.01$.

relative size of one coefficient against another; the levels are in

decays monotonically, that per capita income keeps its sign and does not, and
that manufacturing employment is indistinguishable from zero at all three rungs

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\begin{threeparttable}
\caption{What the estimator did: stopping, conditioning, component scale, and
the variance decomposition}
\label{tab:supp-app-diag}
\footnotesize
\input{../tables/app_tsp_estimator_diag}
\begin{tablenotes}\footnotesize
\item \textit{Notes:} Diagnostics of the fits reported in
\cref{tab:supp-app-ladder}, over the $K\times B=5\times10=50$ fold solves at
each rung, $n=983$. Panel A reports the realised Landweber--Fridman stopping
index $\hat m$ of \cref{def:lfstep}: a solve stopping at $\hat m=1$ returned its
initial condition unchanged, and one reaching the cap $\bar m=15$ was still
descending when it was stopped. The shipped artifact writes that index $\hat m$
here and $\hat m_\varphi$ in \cref{tab:app-phi}; they are the same object,
realised at a $\theta$-step fold solve in this table and at a bootstrap
replication of the $\varphi$-step in that one. Panel B reports the relative residual of the
balancing solve for the representer, the condition number of the moment's
Jacobian $\hat J$ of \eqref{eq:Jhat}, and $\sigma_{\min}(\hat J)$ measured
against $\sigma_{\min}$ of the design second-moment matrix; the last is within
four per cent of one at every rung, so the debiasing term does not degrade
identification and nothing here is a near-singular-Jacobian problem. At $d_Z=0$
the Jacobian is a scalar and its condition number is one by construction, which
is why $\sigma_{\min}$ is reported beside it. Panel C compares the standard
deviation of the fitted structural difference $\Delta\hat\varphi$ and of the
fitted residual $\Delta\hat U$ with that of the outcome they decompose, so an
entry above one is a component larger than the quantity it explains, and reports
the dispersion of the $B$ partition estimates against a robust scale. Panel D
splits the reported standard error into the part that is sampling variation and
the part that is spread across cross-fitting partitions, and repeats the
frontier quantities of \cref{tab:supp-app-feasibility}. \Cref{fig:supp-app-lfpath}
traces the quantity Panel A's stopping index is selected from, which is where
the difficulty of locating that stop is visible. Source:
\texttt{scripts/application/app\_tsp\_02\_ladder.R} and
\texttt{app\_tsp\_common.R}; table
\texttt{paper/tables/app\_tsp\_estimator\_diag.tex}.
\end{tablenotes}
\end{threeparttable}
\end{table}

\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{../figures/app_tsp_lf_path.pdf}
\caption{Landweber--Fridman discrepancy paths, five fold solves}
\label{fig:supp-app-lfpath}
\begin{minipage}{\textwidth}\footnotesize
\textit{Notes:} The quantity the stopping rule of \cref{def:lfstep} thresholds,
traced along the iteration for the five cross-fitting folds of one partition at
the five-control set, $n=983$. The horizontal axis is the iteration index on a
log scale and the vertical axis is the norm of the discrepancy, the difference
between the two periods' fitted transforms; the plotted marker on each series is
where that series stopped. A series whose marker sits at the right-hand edge ran
to the cap $\bar m=15$ and was still descending. The figure is drawn to
show why the stop is hard to locate here rather than to compare folds: three of
the five paths are close to flat over the first decade of iterations, so a
threshold that is slightly too high stops at once and one slightly too low runs
to the cap, which is the behaviour \cref{tab:supp-app-diag} counts. Fold
identities carry no meaning across panels of other figures. Source:
\texttt{scripts/application/app\_tsp\_03\_robustness.R} and
\texttt{app\_tsp\_04\_figures.R}; figure
\texttt{paper/figures/app\_tsp\_lf\_path.pdf}.

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\begin{threeparttable}
\caption{Is N1 imposed? The defect over the class of constant anchors}
\label{tab:app-n1}
\footnotesize
\input{../tables/app_tsp_n1_anchor}
\begin{tablenotes}\footnotesize
\item \textit{Notes:} Chay--Greenstone county panel, $n=983$, at the headline
control set $d_Z=5$, measured on the shipped cross-fitted $\hat L^{(-k)}$ by
replaying the estimation streams of Table 6 of the article rather than on a
reconstruction of it. Every entry is a norm of
$\widehat E[\,\cdot\mid\Delta Z]$ in $L^{2}$, the conditional mean being fitted on
a quadratic basis in $\Delta Z$ of rank $21$, which is the basis that spans the
estimator's own propensity index. ``Entrywise'' is $\max_{j,l}$ over the
$p(\mathsf L-1)$ conditions \cref{cor:centarity} shows N1 to be, eighteen of them
at four cells;
``Contracted, $\varpi_w$ only'' is the single weighted contraction over $l$,
which is the weaker condition; ``Contracted, $\varpi_w\widetilde W$'' is the term
that enters $\psi$, which is conditionally centred under A1 \emph{whatever the
anchor}, and is printed so that an orthogonal-looking moment cannot be read as
evidence for N1. ``Raw'' is the projection norm itself, which at rank $21$ is
dominated by overfitting and is therefore reported only against ``Null floor'',
the $95$th percentile of the same statistic under $300$ permutations of the
observation index in state blocks, which break the dependence between $\hat L$
and $\Delta Z$ the projection is measuring; ``Debiased'' is the HC2-debiased
point estimate and ``$95\%$ upper'' its one-sided upper bound, and those two are
the columns to read. The last column is a permutation $p$ on the largest of the
entries, at the median over the cross-fitting partitions; the draw permutes the
index commonly across cells, so the reference carries the cross-cell dependence
the observed statistic has and the test is multiplicity-correct by construction.
\emph{The reported
defect is minimal over the whole class of constant anchors}, because a projection
on a basis containing an intercept preserves sample means, so no $u$-free,
$\Delta Z$-free constant lowers it and only a genuinely $\Delta Z$-measurable
anchor can. \emph{Nothing is re-anchored and no estimator is changed}; the
$\mathsf L=2$ blocks are the paired arm of Table 6 of the article and the binary
ladder of \cref{tab:supp-app-ladder}, \emph{which differ from each other in
three factors and not in one}, the cross-fitting stream, the truncation level
($\varepsilon_\varrho=0.01$ against $0.03$) and the iteration cap ($\bar m=60$
against $15$), so the two are not a repeated measurement of the binary defect.
Source:
\texttt{scripts/application/app\_tsp\_10\_n1\_anchor.R}; table
\texttt{paper/tables/app\_tsp\_n1\_anchor.tex}.
\end{tablenotes}
\end{threeparttable}
\end{table}
